title: Stable sorts and HashMap's worst case

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: Java sorts an int[] with dual-pivot quicksort but an Integer[] or a List with TimSort. What is the main reason for the difference?

options.text: TimSort is stable, and for objects the order of equal elements can matter.
options.says: Objects are often sorted by one field and then another, so keeping equal elements in order matters; for equal primitives it cannot be observed.

options.text: TimSort is faster, and for objects each comparison can cost a method call.
options.says: The page credits dual-pivot quicksort, not TimSort, with being faster in practice; TimSort is chosen for stability.

options.text: TimSort sorts in place, and for objects the arrays hold references, not values.
options.says: TimSort needs O(n) space for its merge buffer; it is chosen despite that, for stability.

questions.stem: Many keys of a class that does not implement Comparable all have the same hashCode. On Java 21, what is the worst-case cost of get() in that HashMap?

options.text: O(1), because the bucket index comes from the hash, Comparable or not.
options.says: Finding the bucket is O(1), but all the keys share it, so the search inside the bucket decides the cost.

options.text: O(log n), because the bucket becomes a tree even without Comparable.
options.says: The bucket may be treeified, but a tree cannot guide the search among keys that are not Comparable, so the O(log n) bound does not hold.

options.text: O(n), because without Comparable a tree bucket may have to visit each entry.
options.says: Treeification gives O(log n) only when the colliding keys are Comparable; otherwise a lookup can still check every colliding key.

concepts: HashMap is O(1) on average, but many colliding keys make it O(log n) when they are Comparable and O(n) when they are not.
Java sorts objects with TimSort because it is stable, and primitives with dual-pivot quicksort, where stability has no meaning.
